newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO to woo Russia, but fix date for expansion.
newsitem.headline: NATO to woo Russia, but fix date for expansion.

text.p: NATO, emphasising that its eastwards expansion is non-negotiable, will fix a date this week for an "enlargement summit", but offer a pledge to Moscow of no nuclear weapons on the territory of its new members.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher told reporters on Monday that NATO foreign ministers, meeting in Brussels on Tuesday and Wednesday, would also agree an agenda for the summit, likely to take place in mid-July.
"The meeting tomorrow will be significant in setting a date for that NATO summit next year and a full agenda of decisions for that summit," he told reporters.

Diplomatic sources said the summit, also due to approve a reform of alliance command structures and a possible new charter with Russia, would be held in a European capital, probably Madrid. The most likely current dates were July 7 to 9.

Eleven former satellites of the defunct Soviet Union in central and eastern Europe are clamouring to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) -- for years the West's defence bulwark against the now defunct Moscow-led Warsaw Pact.
Russia resolutely opposes plans to expand NATO eastwards, saying it risks creating a new dividing line in Europe.
NATO foreign ministers insist enlargement is firmly on the agenda and in no way negotiable, but they say they want to build a new relationship with their old Cold War foe.

"We want everyone -- the NATO allies, the partner countries, Russia -- to emerge from the summit feeling more secure...but there is no question of a Russian veto (on enlargement)," one senior alliance envoy said.
Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic are the three countries most likely to be asked to open membership talks, but Slovenia and Romania are also in the frame, diplomats say.

NATO Secretary General Javier Solana will also be authorised to open a formal dialogue with Russia over a new NATO-Russia charter governing all aspects of the relationship between the former Cold War foes.
As a first stage, NATO is pushing Moscow to accept the exchange of military liasion officers at NATO's military headquarters and Russia's Ministry of Defence.
The ministers will also review plans to send a new alliance force of between 25,000-30,000 to Bosnia next year to police the fragile Dayton peace accords.
NATO's 16 ambassadors provisionally approved the plan to replace the existing Implementation Force (IFOR) with a Stabilisation Force (SFOR) at a meeting in Brussels earlier on Monday.
They took the decision after meeting representatives of 17 non-NATO nations contributing troops to the peace mission.
The new 18-month alliance-led mission in Bosnia will start on December 20 -- the day the mandate of the current IFOR force expires. REUTER
